extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and readers seeking an overview of narration and point of view in literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on narrating stories: how to choose who tells the story (narrator/voice) and how it is told (tense and technique), with descriptions and examples of common narrative modes and devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration is the use of a written or spoken commentary to convey a story to an audience. Narration is conveyed by a narrator: a specific person, or unspecified literary voice, developed by the creator of the story to deliver information to the audience, particularly about the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narration is a required element of all written stories (novels, short stories, poems, memoirs, etc.), presenting the story in its entirety. It may be optional in other storytelling formats (films, plays, games) where story can be conveyed through dialogue or visual action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative mode (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative mode encompasses the set of choices through which the creator develops their narrator and narration: narrative point of view (person/perspective/voice), narrative tense, and narrative technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three axes — who tells the story (point of view), when/tense it is told (past/present/future), and which techniques (setting, character development, theme, plot structure, linguistic style, devices) — to shape narration and its effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative point of view / perspective / voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of grammatical person used by the narrator to establish whether or not the narrator and the audience are participants in the story; also includes the scope of information or knowledge the narrator presents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point of view determines narrator-audience relationship and information scope; theoretical approaches define POV in terms of person, perspective, voice, consciousness and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative tense
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of either the past or present grammatical tense to establish either the prior completion or current immediacy of the plot (the future tense is also possible but rare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past tense is by far the most common for written literature and can denote distant or immediate past. Present tense gives immediacy; 'historical present' can narrate past events as current. Future tense often creates a prophetic tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative technique (methods to narrate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any of the various other methods chosen to help narrate a story, such as establishing the story's setting (location in time and space), developing characters, exploring themes, structuring the plot, intentionally expressing certain details but not others, following or subverting genre norms, employing certain linguistic styles and using various other storytelling devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select techniques to support desired effects (e.g., reveal/withhold information, follow/subvert genre expectations). Examples and lists of techniques are many (see stream-of-consciousness, unreliable narration, framing, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: A first-person point of view reveals the story through an openly self-referential and participating narrator, using pronouns like I and me (or we/us).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First person creates a close relationship between the narrator and reader. It is often associated with potential unreliability and subjectivity; can be a single narrator or part of alternating first-person narrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-person narration recounts experience using the second-person pronoun you, often adding distance or irony; it can mimic addressed-reader devices but is not always a literal address to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second person can produce effects similar to first-person unreliability and is used in works like Bright Lights, Big City, Italo Calvino's If on a winter's night a traveler, and some sections of N. K. Jemisin's The Fifth Season. It is also common in gamebooks and interactive fiction where the text addresses the player-character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: In third-person narrative mode, narration refers to characters with third-person pronouns (he, she, etc.) and avoids first- or second-person pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-person can be omniscient or limited/close, and can shift among characters in different sections/chapters; it is a flexible default for many novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omniscient vs limited (scope of knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omniscient point of view is presented by a narrator with an overarching perspective, seeing and knowing everything in the story world (including characters' thoughts/feelings). Limited (or close) third-person confines perspective to one character's viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omniscience was typical in nineteenth-century fiction (e.g., Dickens, Tolstoy, George Eliot). Limited/close third-person provides intimate but bounded access to a character (example: J.M. Coetzee's Disgrace). Multiple POV sections can alternate these scopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective vs objective narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective point of view conveys the thoughts, feelings and opinions of one or more characters; objective point of view tells a story without describing characters' inner states, providing an unbiased view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective narration relies on external actions and dialogue; subjective narration opens interiority and bias. Choice affects reader alignment and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating or multiple narrators / multiperspectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works employ multiple points of view presented in discrete sections or chapters, alternating between first-person narrators or between first- and third-person modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple narrators can illustrate various characters' storylines and build complex perspectives (examples: The English Patient; A Song of Ice and Fire series). Multiperspectivity can be interpretive, revealing social identity and the impact on overarching narrative (e.g., framed stories like One Thousand and One Nights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uspensky's five planes of point of view expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Boris Uspenskij identifies five planes on which point of view is expressed in a narrative: spatial, temporal, psychological, phraseological and ideological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these planes to analyze how POV is constructed: spatial (where), temporal (when), psychological (mental life/behaviour), phraseological (language choices), ideological (values/worldview).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological point of view (Lanser)
rubrics_metrics.description: The psychological point of view focuses on the characters' behaviors and encompasses the narrator's distance or affinity to each character and event as represented in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aspect is complex because it deals with narrator-character relational stance; it affects how much interiority is represented and reader empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological point of view (Lanser)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideological point of view focuses on the norms, values, beliefs and worldview of the narrator or a character; it may be explicit or embedded at deep-structural levels and is the most basic yet least accessible to formalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideology can be stated outright or embedded; analysis often relies on intuitive understanding since deep-structural ideology is hard to formalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense-specific effects (past, present, future)
rubrics_metrics.description: Past tense depicts events before the narrator's present (most common); present tense depicts events as occurring in the narrator's current moment and gives immediacy; future tense portrays events after the narrator's present and often sounds prophetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present tense is common in conversational narratives and some modern novels (e.g., Hunger Games). Screenplay action is written in present tense. Choose tense according to desired immediacy, perspective, and stylistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Stream of consciousness attempts to replicate the thought processes of a narrative character, often as interior monologue with incomplete thoughts, desires, and fragmented cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically used in first-person and interior narratives; examples include Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury, Woolf and Joyce (Ulysses). Use to convey interiority and fragmented mental states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable narration involves the use of an untrustworthy narrator; it may create deliberate disbelief or mystery about what is true in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often first-person; third-person may also be unreliable. Example: Holden Caulfield in The Catcher in the Rye, whose bias and emotional immaturity lead to partial or selective disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and story-within-a-story (frame narratives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing encloses stories within a larger narrative (a story told by a storyteller within the main story), connecting discrete tales via a framing device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in oral and literary traditions (e.g., One Thousand and One Nights) to link narratives and to allow variation and adaptation to different audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral-tradition variability and audience tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: In oral storytelling, narratives are often told by multiple elders or storytellers and are shaped by the relationship between narrator and audience, leading to countless variations; narrators may incorporate minor changes to tailor stories to different audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that oral narratives prioritize adaptability and audience engagement; written practice can borrow this approach when considering narrator reliability, voice, and adaptive details.
